Thirty-Nine Articles
THUR-tee-nyn AR-ti-kuhlz
proper noun
The doctrinal confession of the Church of England, finalized in 1571; thirty-nine articles of religion.

📖 Biblical Definition

The Thirty-Nine Articles of Religion are the doctrinal confession of the Church of England, finalized in 1571, which set the reformed and Protestant character of the English church over against Rome on the one hand and against the radical sects on the other. In their best and clearest articles they confess truly Reformation doctrine: the sufficiency of Holy Scripture for salvation, so that nothing is to be required as an article of faith that is not read therein nor may be proved thereby; justification by faith only, declared a most wholesome doctrine and very full of comfort; the bondage of the will and the necessity of grace; predestination and election as the everlasting purpose of God; and the rejection of Roman errors—the sacrifice of the mass, purgatory, transubstantiation, the invocation of saints, and the like—as repugnant to the Word of God. On these heads the Articles stand within the Reformed confessional family, kin to the continental confessions. Yet the English settlement retained an episcopal government and a prescribed liturgy that the Puritans and nonconformists judged to fall short of a thorough reformation according to the Word; and the comprehensiveness designed to hold together varied parties has allowed later readings that strain against the Articles’ plain Protestant sense. The dictionary honors the Thirty-Nine Articles for their clear confession of Scripture’s sufficiency, justification by faith alone, sovereign grace, and the rejection of Roman corruptions, while noting that the English settlement’s retained ceremonies and prelacy were the very points the nonconformists could not in conscience accept.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The doctrinal confession of the Church of England (1571); clear on Scripture’s sufficiency, justification by faith, and sovereign grace, yet retaining ceremonies the Puritans refused.

THIRTY-NINE ARTICLES, the doctrinal confession of the Church of England (1571).

Confess the sufficiency of Scripture for salvation.

Justification by faith only, a most wholesome doctrine.

Affirm predestination and reject Roman errors as repugnant to Scripture.

Retained prelacy and ceremonies the Puritans could not accept.

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The Articles are read either as crypto-Catholic or as a dead formality; their plain sense is Reformation doctrine, though the English settlement kept ceremonies the Puritans refused.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption is the later reading, pressed by the Anglo-Catholic movement, that strains the Articles toward Rome—reinterpreting their plain Protestant statements on justification, the mass, and the sacraments in a Catholic sense their framers expressly excluded. The Articles themselves resist this: they call the Romish doctrine of purgatory, pardons, and the adoration of images a fond thing vainly invented, and the sacrifices of masses blasphemous fables; their justification by faith only (Rom 3:28) is the Reformation’s, not Trent’s.

The principle to recover is the genuinely Reformed substance of the Articles, held alongside the honest reservations of the nonconformists. The Articles confess the sufficiency of Scripture, able to make wise unto salvation (2 Tim 3:15); justification by faith alone; the sovereign election of God before the foundation of the world (Eph 1:4); and the rejection of Roman corruption—real Reformation doctrine, kin to the continental confessions. Yet the English settlement retained an episcopal government and prescribed ceremonies that the Puritans, searching the Scriptures (Acts 17:11), judged to fall short of a thorough reformation by the regulative principle. The dictionary receives the Articles’ clear confession of grace and refuses both the Romeward distortion and the dead formality into which a state-church confession may decline.
